title: FP = #P from \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\)
formal:
Does the following implication hold for ordinary uniform Turing computation?
\[\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\#\mathrm P\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}.\]
The conclusion means exact deterministic polynomial-time computation of every polynomially verifiable witness count, output as a binary nonnegative integer. Since \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\subseteq\#\mathrm P\) holds unconditionally, the conclusion is also written \(\#\mathrm P=\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\).
why: The implication isolates the computational gap between learning that solutions exist and determining their exact number. A proof from the decision-collapse hypothesis would connect two central forms of computational tractability, while a negative answer would show that exact counting can remain hard even after all NP existence problems become easy.
status_note: The checked 2007 draft and 2017 author survey explicitly treat the implication as unresolved. Alasli’s 23 March 2026 v1 claims a positive proof. A direct editorial check on 16 September 2026 finds that its §3.2 uses unsatisfiable formulas with positive second Betti number, incompatible with the solution-complex definition in §2.4. The claim is therefore not accepted as establishing resolution here; this observation does not refute the mathematical conclusion. No independent validation or exhaustive current-status certification is claimed, so status remains uncertain.

sentences: The question asks whether P = NP forces exact polynomial-time computation of every #P witness count.
Each counting function has its own uniform deterministic machine, and its exact value must be output in binary.
Finding one witness or approximating an exponential count to inverse-polynomial relative accuracy does not give its exact value.
The literal negative answer would require P = NP together with a counting function outside numerical FP.
A 2026 preprint claims the implication, but a directly checked internal defect prevents this review from accepting it as a resolution.

definitions:
All language inputs are finite binary strings, of bit length \(n=|x|\). A deterministic polynomial-time machine has a finite program and halts on every input within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps of a multitape Turing machine, for fixed positive integers \(C,d\). Each tape read, write and head move is charged; writing an output is part of the bound. There is no advice, randomness or oracle. The program and constants may depend on the fixed problem, but not on the input. A language belongs to \(\mathrm P\) when such a machine outputs its exact membership bit.

For a fixed polynomial \(p:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with nonnegative integer coefficients and a deterministic verifier \(V(x,y)\) running in time polynomial in \(|x|+|y|\), put
\[W_{V,p}(x)=\{y\in\{0,1\}^{p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1\},\qquad f_{V,p}(x)=|W_{V,p}(x)|.\]
The class \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of languages \(\{x:W_{V,p}(x)\ne\varnothing\}\). The class \(\#\mathrm P\) consists of the total numerical functions \(f_{V,p}\). The verifier is required to halt on every pair of binary strings. Witnesses have exactly the specified length; each distinct witness string contributes one, even when several describe the same object. The hypothesis \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) asserts equality of these language classes, with a separate polynomial-time decider permitted for each language.

The class \(\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\) consists of total functions from binary strings to \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\) computed by deterministic polynomial-time machines under the same bit-cost convention. The output is the exact binary integer, with 0 represented by a single zero and no leading zeros for positive integers. Every \(\#\mathrm P\) function satisfies \(f_{V,p}(x)\leq2^{p(n)}\), so polynomially many output bits suffice. Conversely, a polynomial-time numerical function is in \(\#\mathrm P\): choose a fixed polynomial witness length longer than its output bound, regard witnesses as binary integers, and accept exactly those smaller than its value. This explains the numerical FP equality convention in the source.

In the conclusion the quantifiers are \(\forall V,p\ \exists M,C,d\ \forall x\): one exact counting program for every fixed witness-counting function. No common exponent or effective transformation from arbitrary existence deciders to counting machines is required. The proposition is an implication about these unrelativized classes. It does not assert that P = NP actually holds, introduce access to a SAT oracle, or restrict the algorithms to a specified proof technique.

The logical negation of the target is \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) together with \(\#\mathrm P\not\subseteq\mathrm{FP}_{\mathbb N}\). In particular, a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) would prove the implication through its false antecedent, not refute it. Here and below exact computation differs from relative approximation: an approximation \(a\) with parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1\) need only satisfy \(|a-f(x)|\leq\varepsilon f(x)\), which forces \(a=0\) when the count is zero.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed implication, or of its logical negation. A direct affirmative proof may assume \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) and derive an exact deterministic polynomial-time counting machine for every fixed verifier; a proof of \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\) also settles the literal implication affirmatively. A negative answer must establish both \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) and a \(\#\mathrm P\) function outside numerical FP. An oracle-relative counterexample, a limitation of one proposed reduction, or an error in a claimed affirmative proof does not establish that negation. Approximation, finding a single witness and time polynomial in the numerical count do not meet the exact-computation conclusion.

source_formulation.text: Would P = NP imply polynomial-time exact computation of every #P function?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the explicit question in §9.1 and the exact-counting caveat after Exercise 6 in the January 2007 draft.

context_blocks.text: The known reverse implication is immediate: an exact count decides whether a witness exists by testing whether the value is positive. This card asks whether decision tractability forces counting tractability as well. It is separate from the unconditional question whether all counting functions are already efficiently computable.

Under P = NP, one can find a witness by fixing its bits successively and testing whether each chosen prefix still extends to an accepted witness. The number of prefix queries is polynomial. Running that process for every witness can still require exponential time, because polynomial-time verification allows exponentially many witnesses.

A tempting binary search asks whether \(f(x)\geq k\), with \(k\) encoded in binary. Listing \(k\) distinct witnesses certifies the threshold only at a cost proportional to \(k\), which can be exponential in the input length. Therefore this certificate does not place all binary-threshold questions in NP. An efficient threshold procedure would recover the count with polynomially many comparisons, but P = NP alone does not supply that procedure.

The source and Aaronson’s survey record a substantial weaker consequence: P = NP gives polynomial-time relative approximation at every fixed inverse-polynomial accuracy. Such accuracy need not distinguish adjacent exponential-size counts. Requesting exponentially small relative error can destroy a running-time guarantee polynomial in inverse accuracy, so this known result does not settle exact computation.

The stronger hypothesis P = PSPACE suffices for exact counting. Here PSPACE means decision problems solvable with polynomial working space: exhaustive counting stores a witness and a binary counter of polynomial length, and individual output-bit questions use only polynomial space. The source explicitly separates this implication from the P = NP question.

A March 2026 preprint claims the affirmative implication. A direct editorial check finds an internal obstruction: §2.4 defines \(S(F)\) using precisely the satisfying assignments of a formula, so an unsatisfiable formula gives the empty complex and has \(\beta_2(S(F))=0\), where the second Betti number is the dimension of second homology. Yet §3.2 uses unsatisfiable instances in a family with \(\beta_2=2^{\Omega(N)}>0\). That step cannot hold under the stated definition. This identifies a defect in the presented argument; it neither disproves the implication nor substitutes for a community assessment of the preprint.
